title: AMP results set to offer clues on future strategy
full_text:
AMP reports its half-year results on Thursday, and beyond the numbers, investors and dealmakers will be listening carefully for any signal about the wealth manager’s strategic intentions.
This includes whether a move on Colonial First State remains a live possibility, and what, if anything, it plans to do with its bank.
The speculation has been doing the rounds, though sources have grown more cautious about how far any of it has progressed.
What is less in doubt is that the conditions for a conversation exist. AMP has never made a secret of wanting to sell its bank.
The stumbling block has been that the $5bn financial group wants a price above book value, and buyers have consistently baulked at paying up for a lender carrying a $23bn residential mortgage book competing in a market dominated by the big four.
The bank is capital heavy and its contribution to group earnings fell 9.8 per cent to $55m in 2025. Strip it out, and AMP has a cleaner story to tell.
Whether Thursday’s result offers any clues on that front will be closely watched.
So too will any commentary around capital allocation, particularly given AMP shares are trading at a five-year high, up more than 100 per cent, giving the company a substantially stronger currency should it choose to move on anything.
The arrival of former Jefferies investment banker Jackie Cleary as chief financial officer has added at least the organisational capacity to think seriously about a deal, even if chief executive Blair Vernon struck a cautious tone on mergers and acquisitions at the Macquarie conference in May, signalling a preference for organic growth.
AMP’s $150m on-market buyback was read by Citi analysts as a further sign that large-scale mergers and acquisitions had been shelved.
Yet the industrial logic of a Colonial First State combination is hard to entirely dismiss.
AMP already operates one of the country’s leading wealth platforms in North. CFS, with its master trust at the core, would dramatically accelerate its position in superannuation and funds administration.
For AMP, CFS could be the answer to the question of where growth comes from. Whether AMP is the buyer or becomes a target is the other thread in the speculation.
The more unconventional scenario has KKR, frustrated by the difficulty in finding a buyer for CFS at its price expectations, turning the equation on its head and acquiring AMP instead.
KKR could gain access to AMP’s wealth management distribution network, a natural home for CFS, and then sell the bank separately.
KKR purchased 55 per cent of CFS from Commonwealth Bank in 2020 for $1.7bn and has been working to exit the investment.
Layering in an AMP acquisition would substantially extend its exposure to the Australian wealth management sector rather than reduce it, which is a complication that is hard to ignore.
The CFS sale process, has been described as tailored, language widely read as signalling flexibility around structure.
Thursday’s result may not resolve any of this. But the commentary around the bank, capital deployment and the growth outlook will at least offer a clearer read on where AMP’s head is at – and whether a deal of this scale is genuinely on the agenda or firmly off it.
